disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of excessive motor activity, restlessness, impulsive actions, and difficulty inhibiting behavior, with relatively fewer or less prominent inattentive symptoms. It typically has onset in childhood, but may only become clinically recognized later when environmental demands for sustained self-control increase, such as in structured work or academic settings. The course is often chronic, with some individuals showing partial remission or a shift in symptom expression (e.g., from overt running/climbing to an internal sense of restlessness) across the lifespan. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or personality disorders by its early onset, pervasive pattern across settings, and the specific clustering of hyperactive and impulsive behaviors rather than episodic or situational overactivity.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Charles was promoted to oversee several buildings instead of just working one route, which meant longer staff meetings, more paperwork, and stricter safety audits that demanded sustained sitting and careful sequencing of tasks. He had always been known as the talkative, constantly moving "go-to guy," but the expanded supervisory role left less room for his usual hands-on style and more time confined to a desk and scheduled briefings. Over the following months, coworkers and his supervisor began to comment that he seemed unable to stay in meetings, frequently popped up during trainings, and had trouble sticking with the new scheduling software, which led to missed inspection windows and complaints from building managers. After a tense performance review where his job security was questioned and his wife pointed out similar difficulties sitting through church and bingo nights, he was referred by his primary care doctor to a psychiatrist to evaluate whether there was an underlying condition contributing to his long-standing but now work-impairing restlessness.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t sit still in these meetings or trainings anymore—I feel like I’ve got to get up and move even when everyone else is fine staying put.”

narrative.stressor: Cynthia’s symptoms became more noticeable after she moved into a senior living complex 17 months ago, following a brief hospitalization for a mild heart issue that led her family and doctors to recommend closer monitoring. The new environment imposed fixed schedules for meals, activities, and medication rounds, and staff repeatedly asked residents to remain seated during group programs and health education sessions. Cynthia, who had always thrived on moving between her garden, art table, and volunteer projects, found herself increasingly frustrated by expectations that she stay in one place and wait quietly, which led to gentle but frequent redirections from staff during yoga class, art groups, and community meetings. Concerned that her difficulty settling might be mistaken for agitation or early cognitive decline, her daughter requested a psychiatric evaluation to better understand the longstanding, but now more disruptive, pattern of restlessness in this more structured care setting.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Whenever we’re supposed to sit and do quiet activities here, I just can’t seem to keep myself still and focused on them.”

narrative.stressor: Jorge entered his radiologic technology program 17 months ago, transitioning from a more flexible high school routine into tightly scheduled labs, lectures, and clinical rotations that required careful adherence to protocols and respectful pacing during patient interactions. While his artistic and technical skills with imaging flourished, instructors repeatedly noted that he rushed through instructions, jumped into procedures before being fully briefed, and had difficulty staying in his seat during long lectures and safety trainings, which raised concerns about patient safety and professional conduct. Over the next year, these issues escalated: he received written warnings for interrupting supervisors, cutting off patients mid-explanation, and struggling to wait during team huddles, ultimately being told that his spot in the program might be at risk if he couldn’t regulate his behavior. Feeling distressed that his dream career in radiology was jeopardized and after a clinical preceptor suggested that his lifelong tendency to be "on the go" might reflect more than just nerves, he agreed to see a psychiatrist through the college health service.
narrative.chief_complaint: “In class and in the hospital, I keep jumping in and answering or talking before people even finish their questions, and it’s getting me into trouble.”
